Narad Kumar Das, executive engineer of the Planning and Development Department (PDD), is currently posted at Munger. The EOU team carried out simultaneous searches at five locations in Patna, Muzaffarpur, Bhagalpur and Munger in connection with a disproportionate assets case registered against Das under Section 13(2) and Section 1
news.full_article_text: Bihar EOU recovers ₹52 lakh cash, ₹35 lakh ornaments from executive engineer’s premises EOU team carried out simultaneous searches at 5 locations in Patna, Muzaffarpur, Bhagalpur and Munger in connection with case registered against Bihar government executive engineer The Economic Offences Unit (EOU) on Thursday recovered around ₹ 52 lakh in cash, jewellery worth ₹ 35 lakh and property documents relating to assets worth around ₹ 2 crore during searches at premises linked to a Bihar government executive engineer in a disproportionate assets case, officials said. Narad Kumar Das, executive engineer of the Planning and Development Department (PDD), is currently posted at Munger. The EOU team carried out simultaneous searches at five locations in Patna, Muzaffarpur, Bhagalpur and Munger in connection with a disproportionate assets case registered against Das under Section 13(2) and Section 13(1)(b) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The locations included Das’s residences in Bhagalpur and Patna, a flat in Muzaffarpur, a location in Munger and the government office of the Local Area Engineering Organisation, Works Division, in Munger. Deputy inspector general (EOU) Manavjit Singh Dhillon said ₹ 50 lakh in cash was recovered from a flat in Radhika Apartment during a search in Muzaffarpur and was being counted using a machine. “The case was registered based on information received from a “reliable source” regarding assets allegedly acquired by Das beyond his known sources of income. Prima facie evidence has been found of ₹ 83. 53 lakh in assets allegedly acquired beyond his known legitimate sources of income, which is approximately 64.93 per cent above his known income,” said the DIG, adding that the EOU obtained search warrants from the Special Court of Vigilance. The EOU further said that Das joined in 2014 as an assistant engineer in the water resources department and is now on deputation at PDD, while his father-in-law is a retired teacher. In his rented accommodation at Munger, the EOU found ₹ 1.70 lakh in cash, a Hyundai Sportz car, and documents related to the purchase of ornaments. Additionally, the EOU recovered incriminating documents, investments of ₹ 17.15 lakh in LIC and Aditya Birla, and four passbooks. “In 2026, the executive engineer purchase 3.9 dicimal land at Kusumpuram under Rupaspur police station area on the name of his motherp-in-law Bina Vidyarthi, but the bank records of Das’s wife shows that amounts has been transfered at many times,” the official added. The anti-corruption agency will provide further details after the operation is over and the raiding teams return to Patna. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Avinash Kumar Avinash, a senior correspondent, reports on crime, railways, defence and social sector, with specialisation in police, home department and other investigation agencies.

news.headline: Zambia signs US health deal after disputes over data-sharing
news.story_lead: Zambian Health Minister Roma Chilengi (second right) said the agreement would not allow the sharing of individual patient records - Published 2 hours ago Zambia has signed a five-year health financing agreement with the US, ending months of public dispute over whether the country was trading citizens' medical data and mineral rights for aid. Under the memorandum of understanding, signed in Lusaka on Thursday along with a data-sharing deal, the US will provide about $1.5bn (Â£1.1bn), with Zambia also contributing. Civil society groups had criticised a leaked draft they said allowed too much data sharing, while activists seized on reports that health money was being linked to preferential access for US companies to minerals, which the then-US ambassador denied.
news.full_article_text: Zambian Health Minister Roma Chilengi (second right) said the agreement would not allow the sharing of individual patient records - Published 2 hours ago Zambia has signed a five-year health financing agreement with the US, ending months of public dispute over whether the country was trading citizens' medical data and mineral rights for aid. Under the memorandum of understanding, signed in Lusaka on Thursday along with a data-sharing deal, the US will provide about $1.5bn (Â£1.1bn), with Zambia also contributing. Civil society groups had criticised a leaked draft they said allowed too much data sharing, while activists seized on reports that health money was being linked to preferential access for US companies to minerals, which the then-US ambassador denied. The deal comes after the US Agency for International Development (USAID) was cut. US President Donald Trump had accused USAID of wasteful spending. After closing the agency last year, Washington has pursued similar deals with a number of African countries, arguing partner governments should take on more of the cost. Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda are among those that have signed. Ghana and Zimbabwe have rejected agreements over conditions about sharing data and specimens. Officials say the revised text of Zambia's new deal addresses concerns about privacy, intellectual property and benefit-sharing. Health Minister Roma Chilengi said earlier this week that clauses requiring Zambia to send biological specimens to the US had been removed, and that the agreement would not allow the sharing of individual patient records. Data exchange, he said, would be limited to information needed to monitor and evaluate programmes funded under the deal. - Why some African nations are turning down Trump aid money Published 7 July A draft leaked earlier this year prompted civil society groups to warn that Zambia was accepting wider data-sharing terms than other African countries, including long-term access to pathogen information and specimens. The Chapter One Foundation, a human rights group, said the government risked "signing away" citizens' health data. HIV advocates, including the Treatment Advocacy and Literacy Campaign, said the flow of information would be one-way and demanded the text be published. Opposition figures and activists also seized on reports that health money was being linked to preferential access for US companies to Zambia's large reserves of copper and other critical minerals. In May, Foreign Minister Mulambo Haimbe called the data terms a violation of privacy and "unconscionable", and accused Washington of tying the package to minerals. Then-US ambassador, Michael Gonzales, rejected that account as false. The row was sharpened by an earlier US suspension of drug funding after the embassy alleged theft of donated medicines, which the government disputed. Zambia's new deal replaces support that for years flowed largely through US programmes. The money is intended to support HIV/Aids, tuberculosis, malaria, maternal and child health, disease surveillance and wider health system work, including the recruitment of community health workers. The US has described the arrangement as a shift from a donor-recipient model towards shared responsibility, with US funding expected to decline over the five years as Zambia increases domestic spending. Officials have put the combined package covering 2026 to 2030 at roughly $3.6bn, though figures for the Zambian share have varied. Shortly after taking office for the second time in January 2025, Trump ordered the closure of USAID, in the process decimating health programmes in some African countries that relied on American funding. Critics say the move has impacted the speed of detecting the current ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo and the scale of the response, emphasising that the humanitarian agency was crucial to organising logistics, supplies and local outreach. The US denies its cuts have harmed efforts, arguing that they are more "aligned and effective" under the new arrangement and pointing to the $270m it has donated to tackle the epidemic. Additional reporting by Mallory Moench Related topics More on this story - USAID officially closes, attracting condemnation from Obama and Bush Published 2 July 2025

news.headline: Smoke seen at Riyadh airport; flights cancelled, kindergarten, hospital damaged as tensions escalate
news.story_lead: Smoke seen at Riyadh airport; flights cancelled, kindergarten, hospital damaged as tensions escalate The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by Houthis towards Riyadh and Khamis Mushait. Three people have been killed and 36 injured in attacks on Saudi airports over the past two days, as Yemen's Houthi rebels continued their campaign against the kingdom on Thursday. A fresh barrage targeting Riyadh disrupted airport operations, while missile-interception debris damaged a school and a hospital, Saudi authorities said.
news.full_article_text: Smoke seen at Riyadh airport; flights cancelled, kindergarten, hospital damaged as tensions escalate The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by Houthis towards Riyadh and Khamis Mushait. Three people have been killed and 36 injured in attacks on Saudi airports over the past two days, as Yemen's Houthi rebels continued their campaign against the kingdom on Thursday. A fresh barrage targeting Riyadh disrupted airport operations, while missile-interception debris damaged a school and a hospital, Saudi authorities said. Saudi Civil Defence said fragments from an intercepted ballistic missile fell in Riyadh and caused material damage to a kindergarten and a medical clinic complex. It did not report any casualties from the debris. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched towards Riyadh and another fired towards Khamis Mushait in southwestern Saudi Arabia , near the Yemen border. Deep Dive The Houthis claimed responsibility for the latest attack, saying they targeted King Khalid International Airport with a ballistic missile. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed the strike disrupted airport operations, AP reported. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm that the airport itself had been directly hit. news.headline: Days after narrating drought plight to minister, Maharashtra farmer ends life by jumping in well
news.story_lead: Days after narrating drought plight to minister, Maharashtra farmer ends life by jumping in well Rajendra Sapate, a resident of Dhop taluka in Mohadi, jumped into a well in a paddy field between 8am and 9am, he said. A 55-year-old farmer who spoke of his dire straits during a ministerial visit to review drought conditions a few days earlier allegedly committed suicide on Thursday in Maharashtra's Bhandara district due to distress over crop failure amid lack of rains, an official said. A video being circulated on social media showed Sapate telling Bhandara guardian minister Pankaj Bhoyar about the severe distress farmers were under due to lack of rains.
news.full_article_text: Days after narrating drought plight to minister, Maharashtra farmer ends life by jumping in well Rajendra Sapate, a resident of Dhop taluka in Mohadi, jumped into a well in a paddy field between 8am and 9am, he said. A 55-year-old farmer who spoke of his dire straits during a ministerial visit to review drought conditions a few days earlier allegedly committed suicide on Thursday in Maharashtra's Bhandara district due to distress over crop failure amid lack of rains, an official said. A video being circulated on social media showed Sapate telling Bhandara guardian minister Pankaj Bhoyar about the severe distress farmers were under due to lack of rains. Deep Dive "Farming is in danger due to lack of irrigation. The situation is such that farmers may give up their lives," he says in the video. Bhoyar had visited the area on October 3 to review drought conditions. Sapate is also heard saying that he had repeatedly followed up and submitted petitions and complaints to get irrigation facilities provided, yet no concrete action has been taken. He rued that such petitions and files for relief are gathering dust. The minister had given Sapate a patient hearing and also acknowledged the gravity of the situation. Bhoyar had also assured that necessary action would be taken. "Sapate's entire paddy crop was damaged due to insufficient rainfall. His body has been recovered from the well. The deceased's relatives have said they do not have any suspicion about the death and do not wish to press charges," an Andhalgaon police station official informed. An accidental death case has been registered and further probe is underway, he added. Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis had met Union Home Minister Amit Shah in New Delhi on Wednesday and sought special financial assistance from the Centre for the state, where nearly 80 per cent of the talukas have been affected by severe drought. Water scarcity is being faced on a large scale by 32 districts, while 80 per cent of the talukas (265 out of 358) appear to be completely affected by drought, Fadnavis had said.

news.headline: ‘Uday Shetty will live on forever’: Iran embassy's tribute to Nana Patekar
news.story_lead: ‘Uday Shetty will live on forever’: Iran embassy's tribute to Nana Patekar Nana Patekar died on Thursday at his residence in Goa after suffering a cardiac arrest. The Iranian embassy in India paid tribute to veteran actor Nana Patekar following his death on Thursday, remembering his much-loved comic character Uday Shetty from Welcome (2007). Track funeral updates “Rest in peace, #NanaPatekar.
news.full_article_text: ‘Uday Shetty will live on forever’: Iran embassy's tribute to Nana Patekar Nana Patekar died on Thursday at his residence in Goa after suffering a cardiac arrest. The Iranian embassy in India paid tribute to veteran actor Nana Patekar following his death on Thursday, remembering his much-loved comic character Uday Shetty from Welcome (2007). Track funeral updates “Rest in peace, #NanaPatekar. A great actor has left us, but Uday Shetty and all his unforgettable characters will live on forever. Om Shanti,” the Iranian embassy said on X. Patekar, one of Indian cinema’s most distinctive actors, died on Thursday at his residence in Goa after suffering a cardiac arrest. He was 75. His son, Malhar Patekar, confirmed his death, while doctors at Manipal Hospital said efforts to revive him were unsuccessful. Patekar was declared dead at around 5:20 am. Deep Dive ALSO READ | Atul Kasbekar says Nana Patekar had prepared firewood for his own funeral with ‘spectacularly morbid humour’ Patekar had messaged a friend at around 2.30 am saying that he was unwell, HT reported earlier. The friend later reached his Goa home at around 4 am and found him in distress before he was taken to hospital. Doctors reportedly attempted continuous CPR, but he could not be revived. A medico-legal procedure and post-mortem were initiated as part of the formalities. Patekar’s family, including his wife Neelakanti Patekar and son Malhar, reached Goa Medical College and Hospital ahead of the post-mortem. Maharashtra has also announced that the veteran actor will be accorded a state funeral in Pune. His body is being brought to Pune, where members of the public will have an opportunity to pay their last respects. The cremation is scheduled to take place at his farmhouse. ALSO READ | Exclusive-Juhi Chawla: Nana Patekar was legendary in his own rustic way From intense dramatic roles to Uday Shetty While Nana Patekar built his reputation through powerful and often intense performances in films such as Parinda, Krantiveer and Ab Tak Chhappan , his portrayal of Uday Shetty in Anees Bazmee’s 2007 comedy Welcome introduced another side of the actor to a mass audience. Uday Shetty, a gangster desperate to get his sister married into a respectable family, was written as a volatile, intimidating figure who repeatedly found himself caught up in absurd situations. Patekar played the character with the same intensity that had defined many of his serious roles but channelled it into comedy. news.headline: After IndiGo, Air India and Akasa raise fuel costs amid ATF spike
news.story_lead: After IndiGo, Air India and Akasa raise fuel costs amid ATF spike The latest fuel price hike has further raised airline operating costs, with fuel continuing to account for a substantial share of overall airline expenditure. Air India Group, on Thursday, announced that it would increase fuel surcharge across its domestic and select international routes in response to the continued increase in Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) prices. “The revised fuel surcharge will be reflected in the fare applicable to new bookings made from 0000 Hrs IST on 9 October for Air India Express, and from 1100 hrs IST on 9 October for Air India.
news.full_article_text: After IndiGo, Air India and Akasa raise fuel costs amid ATF spike The latest fuel price hike has further raised airline operating costs, with fuel continuing to account for a substantial share of overall airline expenditure. Air India Group, on Thursday, announced that it would increase fuel surcharge across its domestic and select international routes in response to the continued increase in Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) prices. “The revised fuel surcharge will be reflected in the fare applicable to new bookings made from 0000 Hrs IST on 9 October for Air India Express, and from 1100 hrs IST on 9 October for Air India. The surcharge varies by sector and route category,” the Air India spokesperson said. Also read | Patna-Lucknow IndiGo flight’s nose suffers damage, lightning strike among suspected causes The latest increase in fuel prices has further elevated operating costs for airlines, with fuel continuing to account for a substantial proportion of overall airline expenditure, the spokesperson added. This comes after the Federation of Indian Airlines (FIA), which represents Air India, IndiGo and SpiceJet, had, on September 25, written to the civil aviation ministry and sought a series of measures from the government to ease the financial pressure on domestic airlines amid the continuing West Asia conflict, higher aviation fuel prices, airspace restrictions and rupee depreciation. The spokesperson said that Air India and Air India Express have undertaken a “calibrated revision” of fuel surcharges, with the adjustments intended to partially offset the increased cost burden while enabling the two airlines to continue providing reliable and high-quality services across their networks. Revised fuel surcharge The revised fuel surcharge on domestic one-way sectors will be ₹ 400 for flights up to 500 km, ₹ 600 for 501–1,000 km, ₹ 850 for 1,001–1,500 km, and ₹ 1,200 for sectors of 1,501 km and above. Also read | Why is IndiGo hiking fuel charges again? The revised fuel surcharge on international one-way sectors will be USD 215 for North America, USD 210 for Australia, USD 135 for Europe including the UK and USD 55 for West Asia/Middle East. Akasa Air, too, announced a revision in its fuel charge attributing to the sustained increase in ATF prices. “The revised fuel surcharge will be applicable to all new bookings made with effect from 00:01 hrs on October 9, 2026 onwards. ATF constitutes a significant component of airline operating costs, and the continued increase in fuel prices has placed sustained pressure on airline operating costs across the industry. In view of the prevailing fuel price environment, Akasa Air has taken a measured approach to partially offset the impact,” its spokesperson said. Akasa Air’s fuel surcharge on domestic routes will be ₹ 375 for sectors up to 500 km, ₹ 600 for 501–1,000 km, ₹ 900 for 1,001–1,500 km, and ₹ 1,150 for sectors of 1,501 km and above. On international routes, a fuel surcharge of ₹ 2,500 will apply on flights between India and Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Thailand and Vietnam. “Akasa Air will continue to monitor fuel prices and the broader operating environment and review the fuel surcharge periodically,” the spokesperson said. IndiGo, the country's largest airline, also increased fuel charges on October 5 with effect from October 6. Under the revised structure, fuel charges on domestic routes have been increased to ₹ 375 for flights up to 500 km, ₹ 600 for flights up to 1000km, ₹ 900 for flying between 1001 to 1500km, ₹ 1,150 for flights operating for a distance up to 2,000 km and ₹ 1,300 for flights beyond 2,000 km. For international flights, the charges are fixed at ₹ 1,000 for SAARC routes up to 500 km and ₹ 3,000 for those beyond 500 km. Flights to Southeast Asia, the Gulf and Middle East countries and North and East Asia will have a charge of ₹ 5,500. The fuel charge for Africa will be ₹ 6,000 and ₹ 10,000 for Europe. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Neha LM Tripathi Neha LM Tripathi is a Special Correspondent with the National Political Bureau of Hindustan Times. She covers the aviation and railways ministries, and also writes on travel trends. Her work spans national developments, with a focus on policy, people, and the evolving travel landscape. She has 13 years of experience. Before moving to Delhi, she was based in Mumbai, where she began her journey as a journalist. Outside the newsroom, Neha enjoys trekking and travelling. Read More

news.headline: Elon Musk asks why Starlink still lacks India licence, gets a reply from Rahul Gandhi
news.story_lead: Elon Musk asks why Starlink still lacks India licence, gets a reply from Rahul Gandhi SpaceX CEO Musk noted that while Starlink is licensed in 165 countries, it has spent five years complying with Indian laws and government requirements. Trillionaire Elon Musk on Thursday asked why Starlink was not issued a licence in India yet despite complying with every law for five years. His post received a response from Congress MP Rahul Gandhi .
news.full_article_text: Elon Musk asks why Starlink still lacks India licence, gets a reply from Rahul Gandhi SpaceX CEO Musk noted that while Starlink is licensed in 165 countries, it has spent five years complying with Indian laws and government requirements. Trillionaire Elon Musk on Thursday asked why Starlink was not issued a licence in India yet despite complying with every law for five years. Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi responded to his X post with a cryptic reference to “the other guy”. Gandhi responded to Musk’s post: “Welcome to India, Elon. The ministry said telecom licences had been granted to three companies offering GMPCS services using non-geosynchronous satellite orbits -- Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb, backed by Bharti Airtel, and Jio Satellite Communications. Under the terms of their licences, all three are required to demonstrate compliance with security conditions aimed at ensuring the safety of users and their data, the ministry said. “Security assessment as part of this process is currently under way in respect of all the three licensees,” it said, adding that the companies were at “broadly the same regulatory stage”. The government’s statement did not name Musk or Ambani and did not directly address Musk’s allegation involving the Reliance Industries chairman. At the India Mobile Congress on Wednesday, Starlink vice-president Lauren Dreyer said the company had built its India operations around the country’s security requirements and had established 20 gateway sites comprising hundreds of antennas. “We are ready to serve in India, once India is ready,” she said.
